column2: The rapid proliferation of GPU-accelerated servers has ended the decade-long era of flat data centre energy use (E02 pdf p. 8, ROW-0026). While global data centre compute instances grew 550% between 2010 and 2018 with only a 6% energy increase to ~205 TWh in 2018 (E01 pdf p. 2, ROW-0010, ROW-0011), US data centre electricity consumption surged from 76 TWh in 2018 to 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of total US electricity) and is projected to reach 325 to 580 TWh by 2028 (6.7% to 12.0% of US power) (E02 pdf p. 7-8, ROW-0021, ROW-0023, ROW-0025). Globally, data centre demand is projected to more than double from 415 TWh in 2024 to ~945 TWh by 2030 and ~1,200 TWh by 2035 in the IEA Base Case (E03 pdf p. 14, ROW-0037, ROW-0041, ROW-0042), with 2025 AI accelerator Thermal Design Power (TDP) reaching 6.8 GW for NVIDIA/AMD and up to 12.0 GW total (E04 pdf p. 4, ROW-0061, ROW-0062).
column6: GRP-01, GRP-02, GRP-07
column10: Three independent primary lineage groups: GRP-01 (LBNL server stock modeling), GRP-02 (de Vries-Gao chip supply-chain modeling), and GRP-07 (IEA global energy system balances). Note: E01 and E02 share coauthors (GRP-01); E04 and E05 share the same author (GRP-02).
column12: None. All sources confirm inflection away from flat demand.

column2: Building new high-voltage transmission lines requires 4 to 8 years in advanced economies (E03 pdf p. 15, ROW-0049), and supply-chain wait times for critical grid components such as transformers and cables doubled between 2021 and 2024 (E03 pdf p. 15, ROW-0050), lagging behind the 1 to 2 year deployment cycle of hyperscale facilities. In Virginia, utilities can protect grid reliability by delaying new large customer additions (E06 pdf p. 9, ROW-0090) as unconstrained growth requires adding 3.6 to 3.8 GW/yr of generation and 8.7 GW of transmission transfer capacity between 2025 and 2040 (E07 pdf p. 17-18, ROW-0105, ROW-0107). In India, grid connection approvals slow deployment (E08 pdf p. 4, ROW-0125) with 2 to 3 GW concentrated on the Kalwa/Padghe corridor into Mumbai by 2030 (E09 pdf p. 14, ROW-0150). Illustrative trade press confirms Dominion halted connections in Eastern Loudoun County due to transmission constraints (E13 pdf p. 1, WEB-0016; E14 pdf p. 3, WEB-0020).
column6: GRP-03, GRP-07, GRP-08
column10: Three independent primary lineage groups: GRP-07 (IEA global grid assessment), GRP-03 (Virginia JLARC audit & E3 rate study), and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: FSR Global & CEEW). E06 and E07 count as one group because E07 was prepared for E06. Secondary sources E13 and E14 moved to illustration.
column12: None. Consistent findings across US, Europe, and India.

column2: Data centre electricity demand exhibits extreme spatial concentration in specific nodes: Northern Virginia hosts 13% of global and 25% of Americas operational capacity (E06 pdf p. 5, ROW-0084) carrying ~70% of global internet traffic (E07 pdf p. 23, ROW-0113); in India, Mumbai accounted for ~53% of national operational capacity in 2024 (E09 pdf p. 8, ROW-0143) with 2 to 3 GW concentrated on the Kalwa/Padghe corridor by 2030 (E09 pdf p. 14, ROW-0150) proximal to submarine cable landings (E08 pdf p. 10, ROW-0126); and in Ireland, data centres accounted for 7,663 GWh or 23% of total national metered electricity in 2025 (E16 pdf p. 1, ROW-0175, ROW-0176), exceeding the 18% share consumed by all urban residential dwellings (E16 pdf p. 1, ROW-0178).
column6: GRP-03, GRP-06, GRP-08
column10: Three independent primary lineage groups: GRP-03 (JLARC/E3 Virginia study), GRP-06 (CSO Ireland meter billing census), and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: CEEW & FSR Global, merged due to shared JLL/CBRE market data). Secondary trade and media reports (E15, E17, E19) retained strictly as illustrations.
column12: None. Empirical geographic concentration confirmed by meter data.

column2: Data centres operate with flat, continuous 24/7 load profiles maintaining load factors above 0.85 (versus 0.5-0.6 for typical industry) and power factors of 0.95-0.99 behind double-conversion UPS systems that isolate IT loads from grid disturbances with THD <5% (E09 pdf p. 10, 12, ROW-0145, ROW-0147, ROW-0148). Facilities require a stable, uninterrupted 24/7 power supply (E08 pdf p. 12, ROW-0127) with individual Virginia campuses drawing from 18 MW up to 100-200+ MW each (E06 pdf p. 45, ROW-0096, ROW-0097). Because computational IT load cannot ramp down dynamically to support the grid (E09 pdf p. 16, ROW-0152), grid operators require on-site dispatchable generation or storage matching 100% of Maximum Import Capacity (MIC) (E10_P1 pdf p. 4, ROW-0159) to prevent mandatory demand curtailment.

column10: Four independent primary lineage groups: GRP-07 (IEA load profiling), GRP-03 (JLARC utility metered load), GRP-04 (CRU statutory decision paper), and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: CEEW operator surveys and FSR Global power engineering analysis, merged due to shared commercial market baseline).
column12: None. Electrical baseload profile verified across all jurisdictions.

column2: Large-scale data centre grid additions create ratepayer cost-shifting risks: in Virginia, a residential customer of Dominion Energy could experience monthly bill increases of $14 to $37 by 2040 for generation and transmission infrastructure under unconstrained growth (E06 pdf p. 9, ROW-0091), with large capital expenditures potentially raising utility borrowing costs for existing customers (E07 pdf p. 19, ROW-0111) and rural electric cooperatives facing solvency strain if large loads leave (E06 pdf p. 70, ROW-0102; E07 pdf p. 13, ROW-0120). In India, dual sourcing where data centres contract standby capacity from DISCOMs while wheeling off-grid renewables causes financial stress and fixed-cost socialization for utilities (E08 pdf p. 14, ROW-0131), alongside transmission stranding risks when 200 MW connections shift to 120 MW grid offtake (E09 pdf p. 24, ROW-0155).
column6: GRP-03, GRP-08
column10: Two independent primary lineage groups: GRP-03 (JLARC bill modeling & E3 rate study) and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: CEEW Indian DISCOM financial analysis & FSR Global transmission stranding analysis). Note: E06 and E07 count as one group because E07 was prepared for E06; E08 and E09 merged into GRP-08 due to shared underlying data.
column12: None. Economic cost socialization identified in both US and India.

column2: Regulators are moving from promotional tariff subsidies toward mandatory connection obligations: while state power incentives historically dominated data centre policy in India (E08 pdf p. 4, 18, ROW-0124, ROW-0135), Ireland's Commission for Regulation of Utilities directed system operators to assess data centres as a distinct demand class (E10_P2 pdf p. 3, 5, ROW-0164, ROW-0165) and mandated that new facilities provide on-site dispatchable generation or storage matching 100% of MIC and secure 80% renewable PPAs (E10_P1 pdf p. 4, ROW-0159, ROW-0160). E09 notes India's IEGC lacks technical standards for large electronic loads (pdf p. 26, ROW-0156).
column6: GRP-04, GRP-08
column10: Two independent primary lineage groups: GRP-04 (CRU Ireland statutory decisions E10_P1 and E10_P2) and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: CEEW policy synthesis & FSR Global grid code review). E10_P1 and E10_P2 are one group because both are from CRU Ireland; E08 and E09 merged into GRP-08. Secondary sources E10_S1, E10_S2, E18 kept as illustrations.
column12: None. Shift from promotional incentives to grid-protection rules.

column2: Interconnection queues and developer capacity applications overestimate actual operational demand due to speculative multi-queuing across utility service areas. LBNL notes bottom-up modeling avoids overestimation caused by tracking data centre load across multiple queues (E02 pdf p. 8, ROW-0029). In Virginia, Dominion builds transmission to serve 1,000 MW of forecasted metered load even when customers request 2,000 MW of capacity (E06 pdf p. 69, ROW-0101). In India, commercial load shifts between contracted MW and actual grid draw create planning gaps (E09 pdf p. 24, ROW-0155). Illustrative trade press reports Dominion's contracted queue reached 53.8 GW in July 2026 across its service territory (E15 pdf p. 2, WEB-0022, as reported by a secondary source).
column6: GRP-01, GRP-03, GRP-08
column10: Three independent primary lineage groups: GRP-01 (LBNL utility load analysis), GRP-03 (JLARC Dominion metered vs requested audit), and GRP-08 (Indian DC & Grid Integration Lineage: FSR Global commercial lifecycle analysis). Secondary trade press E15 (53.8 GW queue) excluded from independent count and retained as illustration.
column12: None. Utilities universally report speculative multi-queuing.

column2: High penetrations of inverter-based renewable resources reduce grid rotational inertia (E09 pdf p. 8, ROW-0144). In India, midday solar generation surpluses of ~40 GW caused severe frequency spikes breaching the statutory 50.05 Hz ceiling (reaching 50.39 Hz on August 4 and 50.377 Hz on August 25, 2024 for over 220 minutes) (E09 pdf p. 20, ROW-0153, ROW-0154). Integrating variable data centre renewable demand requires 10 GW of battery storage and 31 GW of hydrogen-capable combustion turbines in Virginia by 2040 (E07 pdf p. 18, ROW-0108), BESS adoption over the next 3 to 5 years in India (E08 pdf p. 14, ROW-0133), and firm clean dispatchable capacity globally (E03 pdf p. 14, ROW-0043).
